svg.title: Map the fictional website name only on this PC — instructional mockup
svg.desc: Step-specific guided recreation. Not a genuine screenshot or live result.
svg.text: INSTRUCTIONAL MOCKUP — NOT A LIVE CAPTURE OR RESULT
Map the fictional website name only on this PC
Your Windows host · Administrator Windows PowerShell
Windows PowerShell — Administrator
COMMAND / FILE CONTENT TO ENTER — PRESERVE CASE
$HostsFile = "$env:SystemRoot\System32\drivers\etc\hosts"
if (!(Test-Path "$HostsFile.sonic-tls-backup")) { Copy-Item $HostsFile "$HostsFile.sonic-tls-backup"
if (!(Select-String -Path $HostsFile -Pattern '\bapp\.example\.mil\b' -Quiet)) { Add-Content -Path
$HostsFile -Value "`r`n10.90.0.10 app.example.mil" }
Select-String -Path $HostsFile -Pattern 'app\.example\.mil'
EXPECTED RESULT / SIMULATED CLUE — CHECK YOUR OWN MACHINE
The hosts-file line maps app.example.mil to 10.90.0.10, and no duplicate conflicting entry
exists.
FOLLOW THE NUMBERED INSTRUCTIONS IN THE LESSON
1. Click Start, type PowerShell, right-click Windows PowerShell, and choose Run as administrator. Accept
the prompt for your own PC.
2. Paste the block. It keeps a backup of the original hosts file if one does not already exist, then
adds a line only if this exact name is not present.
3. Read the final line. It must be 10.90.0.10 app.example.mil. If an older entry maps it elsewhere, open
Notepad as administrator, open the hosts file using All Files, and correct only your lab entry.
4. Close this administrator window when finished. The change affects this PC only; it is not a public
DNS registration.
No real private key, real certificate result, production access or DoD endorsement is shown.
